newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone parliament defies ban to denounce coup.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone parliament defies ban to denounce coup.

text.p: Members of Sierra Leone's dissolved parliament have met in defiance of a ban on political activity to denounce a two-week-old military coup and call for the return of ousted civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.

Fifty members of the 80-seat parliament meeting at Freetown's Miatta Conference Hall on Saturday evening unanimously approved a resolution calling on the military rulers to restore the constitution suspended after the May 25 coup. Several members of parliament have fled the country.
"We the members of parliament unequivocally condemn the overthrow of the constitutionally elected government of Sierra Leone," the resolution said.
It called for urgent implementation of a peace accord signed in November by Kabbah and rebels fighting since 1991, who have now allied with the coupmakers and flooded into Freetown.
"Legitimate grievances of the Armed Forces of Sierra Leone, the Revolutionary United Front and all other aggrieved parties must be immediately addressed," the resolution said.
The coupmakers have been meeting civilian politicians trying to win them over and have proposed a government of national unity. So far no one has accepted.
They have also sent delegations to West African states to explain their actions and win support for their cause.
Regional power Nigeria has built up its troops in Sierra Leone since the coup, and staged an unsuccessful show of force last Monday to try to force the army to back down.
The Armed Forces Revolutionary Council has called on people to demonstrate on Sunday afternoon wearing white shirts as a sign of their opposition to foreign intervention.
Thousands of Freetown residents have fled to the provinces, others have gone by land or sea to neighbouring Guinea and Liberia.

Witnesses said a boat left for the Guinean capital Conakry on Saturday carrying more of Kabbah's ministers to join him in exile, including foreign minister Shirley Gbujama, and tourism and culture minister Yembeh Mansaray. Finance Minister Thaimu Bangura is among those already there.
Many of the Lebanese who dominate the retail trade in the country have fled. Food prices have soared, and basic imported items like rice, sugar and flour, and kerosene and petrol are in short supply.
The central bank was burned down in the coup, and only the black market is operating. The leone currency has fallen from 860 to the dollar before the coup to 1,300 to the dollar now.
The government officially reopened the country's borders on Sunday. An uneasy calm reigned in Freetown, where residents went to church as usual.
The coup leaders say they want a peaceful solution but do not want Kabbah back, accusing him of blocking peace with rebels, humiliating the army and promoting ethnic hatred.
Sierra Leone's West African neighbours have been making diplomatic contacts to decide on their next move.
